I want to understand how a visual cortex that has never seen anything gets
ready to see, and how the first days of visual experience turn that
preparation into a reliable representation of the world. Everything below is
a version of that question. I work on it with recurrent network models of
cortical circuits and with chronically imaged populations of neurons in the
developing ferret visual cortex, and I try to keep the models simple enough to
take apart and the data close enough that the models have to answer to it.

## Structure before experience

The visual cortex is not a blank slate waiting for input. Already before eye
opening, it shows spontaneous activity with a rich spatial organisation:
patterns on the scale of millimetres, repeating with a characteristic
wavelength, correlated across distant parts of the cortical sheet, and
confined to a small number of dimensions. This organisation is generated to a
large part by the cortex's own recurrent circuitry; it persists when the
retina and thalamus are silenced. Work from our group together with the
Fitzpatrick lab, and from several other groups, has shown that the layout of
these spontaneous patterns before eye opening predicts the layout of the
orientation map that the same patch of cortex will have afterwards. The
developing cortex, in other words, has a repertoire of patterns it readily
produces before it has any visual reason to.

I want to know what this endogenous structure is for. One reading is that it
is a scaffold: a set of preferred activity patterns that experience then
selects among and sharpens. Another is that it is a constraint: whatever the
cortex later learns has to be expressible in terms of patterns the network can
already sustain. Both readings make predictions about what should happen at
eye opening, and testing them is the thread running through my work.

## From variable to reliable

Models of cortical development have mostly been built to explain tuning and
map layout: why a neuron prefers one orientation, and why neighbouring
neurons prefer similar ones. They say much less about a property that is
just as important for seeing, namely reliability. If the same stimulus is
shown twice, does the cortex respond the same way twice?

At eye opening it does not. The response to a simple oriented grating varies
strongly from trial to trial, and each response resembles one of the
spontaneous patterns more than it resembles the response to the same grating
a moment later. Over the following days this changes. Responses to the same
stimulus become reproducible, responses to different stimuli become distinct,
and an orientation map emerges that then stays stable. In
*Trägenap et al., Nature Neuroscience 2025* we followed this transition in
individual ferrets, imaging the same region of cortex day after day through
the week after eye opening, and asked what change in the circuit could
account for it.

The explanation that fits the data is not that the cortex becomes quieter or
that its noise goes down. It is that the visual input becomes aligned with the
network's own structure. The recurrent network amplifies some activity
patterns and suppresses others, and reliability emerges once the feedforward
drive for a stimulus comes to lie along the amplified patterns, so that the
network's response to a stimulus and its spontaneous activity begin to agree.
A model in which this alignment is the only thing that changes reproduces the
rise in reliability, the growing match between evoked and spontaneous
patterns, and the time course over days. Models in which the input is merely
strengthened, or the noise merely reduced, do not.
([press release](https://fias.institute/en/news/news-publicity/learning-to-see-a-mix-of-nature-and-nurture/) ·
[free-to-read version](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-024-01857-3.epdf?sharing_token=GwWYQRrz-zub53Fug5n7UdRgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0M7mcLR7y-jFw14-nj_gtm6ywdvYoPVRIr_VUd7JsYV_8IKHS0hYLlzSCcrssR-rATJZeAwYyx6R5SJjIyj4cSPLALkqJbHibiN74JKVL2qsolm3CfkUvDI4TAUomlN-BQ%3D))

I find this result appealing because it recasts the question of nature and
nurture. The cortex arrives with a set of patterns it represents well.
Experience does not have to build a representation from nothing; it has to
bring the input into register with what is already there.

## Feedforward input meets recurrent circuits

This raises the next question: what is the feedforward input itself doing
during that week? With the Fitzpatrick lab we looked at both sides of the
junction, the thalamic input arriving in cortex and the cortical response it
produces, across the same developmental window. In
*Lempel, Trägenap et al., Neuron 2025* we found that coherent cortical
responses develop as two things change together. The feedforward inputs for
different stimuli become more distinguishable from one another, and they
become better aligned with the recurrent network they feed into. Neither
change on its own accounts for the data.
([press release](https://fias.institute/en/news/news-publicity/learning-to-see-is-teamwork/) ·
[doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014))

Part of what makes this hard to study is that two-photon imaging in the
ferret does not reach the thalamic input layer, which lies too deep. So this
work combines imaging of the superficial layers with electrophysiology and
modelling to say something about the layer we cannot see.

## Selective amplification across the cortical sheet

Underneath both results is a claim about the recurrent network: that it
amplifies activity patterns with a particular spatial scale and suppresses
others, acting as a pattern-selective filter. The classic account of how
this could work is local excitation and wider inhibition, which pick out one
wavelength. The Smith lab has tested this directly with patterned optogenetic
stimulation: uniform light evokes modular activity at the network's preferred
wavelength, and patterns at other wavelengths are pulled towards it
(*Mulholland, Kaschube and Smith, 2024*). The
[recurrent networks page](teaching/recurrent-networks.qmd) in the Teaching
section walks through the underlying mechanism in its simplest form.

With the Smith lab I am now asking which patterns the developing cortex
amplifies on the scale of millimetres, how selective that amplification is,
and which recurrent subnetworks can account for it. This is the work in
*Mulholland, Trägenap et al., bioRxiv 2026* (co-first authors;
[doi:10.64898/2026.03.31.715687](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.31.715687)).
One thing we have learned along the way is that a perfectly uniform network of
this kind would be too permissive, sustaining any pattern of the right
wavelength equally well. It is the heterogeneity of real cortex, in connection
strengths and in local anisotropies, that confines activity to a small set of
patterns, and it is this set that the spontaneous activity reveals.

## A detour into skin

For several years, funded by the Center for Multiscale Modelling in
Frankfurt, I also worked on models of pattern formation in the developing
skin of cuttlefish. In the details this is a different subject, but the
models belong to the same family: a field of interacting elements, local
activation and longer-range inhibition, and a pattern with a characteristic
wavelength that emerges from the interactions rather than from a template.
Seeing the same mechanism at work in two systems that share no cells, no
molecules and no evolutionary purpose was a useful reminder that the
explanation lies in the structure of the interactions, not in the particular
biology that implements them.

## Looking ahead: across the animal tree

Most of what we know about cortical development comes from a handful of
species, and these species differ in instructive ways. Carnivores, primates
and tree shrews have smooth orientation maps with a periodic layout and
pinwheels; rodents have the same selectivity but arranged in a salt-and-pepper
fashion, and their spontaneous activity shows none of the low-dimensional,
map-like structure described above. Several hypotheses have been proposed for
why, from cortical size to the density of thalamic afferents to the loss of an
ancestral columnar organisation, and none has settled the matter. By comparing
how the cortex is organised and how it develops across ferrets, cats, tree
shrews and mice, I hope to separate the developmental principles that are
shared from those that belong to one lineage. Where a species departs from the
others, the departure points at the mechanism, and a theory that explains only
one species is not yet a theory of the cortex.

## Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines

The developing cortex solves a problem that artificial systems also face: how
to learn quickly from limited experience. The strategy we see in the brain is
to start from a structured prior, generated by the network's own dynamics, and
to align incoming data with it rather than learn a representation from
nothing. I am curious whether this strategy, made explicit, could make
learning in artificial neural networks faster or more robust, and in the other
direction, whether the tools built for understanding learning in deep networks
can tell us something about what the cortex does in its first week of seeing.

## How I work

I sit between theory and experiment and I like it there. In practice this
means dynamical recurrent network models of cortical circuits, analysis of
large-scale two-photon and widefield calcium imaging data, and the comparison
of the two: a model suggests what to measure, the measurement reshapes the
model, and neither side gets to be right on its own. During my PhD I have done
this in long-running collaborations with the labs of David Fitzpatrick (Max
Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience) and Gordon Smith (University of
Minnesota). Much of what I have learned about doing science well has come
from the friction between the way a theorist and an experimentalist look at
the same figure.

A few habits follow from this. I prefer the simplest model that can be
wrong, because a model I cannot break is a model I cannot learn from. Before
fitting anything, I spend time on the question of what the model predicts
that the data could contradict. And I try to make models playable: the
parameter-exploration notebook linked below and the
[interactive pages](teaching/index.qmd) in the Teaching section exist because
changing a parameter and watching the pattern respond has taught me things
that a derivation did not.
